questions.text: The docs mention `pragma graft_status;`. What other graft_* pragmas does the SQLite extension add, and where is the list defined?
questions.how_found: Grepped for graft_status across the workspace; it lands on the doc comments of the GraftPragma enum in crates/graft-sqlite/src/pragma.rs, which enumerates every supported pragma (volumes, tags, switch, clone, fork, checkout, info, status, snapshot, fetch, pull, push, audit, hydrate, version, import, export, dump_header, dump_commit). The string -> variant parsing is right below in `TryFrom<&Pragma>` (lines 119-175).
questions.why_asked: The pragmas are the whole user-facing control surface of the extension; on day one you want to know what you can actually type at a sqlite3 prompt.

questions.text: Is there a MIN_SQLITE_VERSION_NUMBER that sqlite-plugin requires, and what happens if the SQLite we load into is older than that?
questions.how_found: rg MIN_SQLITE_VERSION_NUMBER -> src/vfs.rs:19 defines it as 3037002 (SQLite 3.37.2). The enforcement is in register_inner: it calls libversion_number() and outright panics with "sqlite3 must be at least version {}, found version {}" if the host is older.
questions.why_asked: Before shipping a VFS extension you need to know the minimum runtime you can target, and whether a too-old host fails loudly or silently misbehaves. (It panics, which is worth knowing.)

questions.text: What is SPLINTER_V2_MAGIC and how does Splinter detect that a serialized buffer is truncated or corrupt?
questions.how_found: rg SPLINTER_V2_MAGIC -> src/codec/footer.rs:9, a 4-byte trailer [0x59,0x11,0xA7,0xE2]. The Footer struct is a little-endian u64 CRC64-NVMe checksum plus that magic; Footer::validate returns DecodeErr::Magic then DecodeErr::Checksum. Cross-checked the call sites in src/codec.rs:252 and src/splinter_ref.rs:247.
questions.why_asked: If you ever have to eyeball a hex dump of a stored bitmap, or debug a decode failure, you need to know the on-disk envelope and which error means what.

questions.text: I see a `__sqlsync_timelines` table appearing in databases. Who creates it and what is stored in it?
questions.how_found: rg __sqlsync_timelines -> lib/sqlsync/src/timeline.rs. TIMELINES_TABLE_SQL creates it (id BLOB PRIMARY KEY, lsn INTEGER, STRICT); run_timeline_migration executes it, called from both LocalDocument::open and CoordinatorDocument::open. It is the per-timeline high-water mark of applied mutations, read/written by rebase_timeline and apply_timeline_range so mutations are never applied twice.
questions.why_asked: An unexplained double-underscore table in a user's database is the first thing you notice when you open a SQLSync db in a GUI, and you need to know whether it's safe to touch.

questions.text: If a database is edited on two machines at once, does the recurring background job resolve the conflict, or is it left for a human to sort out?
questions.how_found: Followed Runtime::new -> supervise(AutosyncTask) -> AutosyncTask::run. On each tick it walks every volume and compares local_changes/remote_changes; when BOTH sides have changes the branch body is empty with the comment 'volume has diverged and requires user/app intervention'. So nothing is merged and nothing is chosen: the volume is simply skipped forever until someone acts. Confirmed by plan_commit in rt/action/remote_commit.rs, which returns LogicalErr::VolumeDiverged in the same situation.
questions.why_asked: This is the first thing anyone asks about an offline-first sync engine: what happens on a genuine concurrent edit. The answer (it silently stalls the volume) is a real operational gotcha.

questions.text: How does SQLSync discover which b-trees a live SELECT touches, so it knows when a subscription has gone stale?
questions.how_found: Traced the reactive path from sqlsync-wasm/src/reactive.rs into lib/sqlsync/src/reactive_query.rs. refresh_state prepares 'EXPLAIN <sql>', walks the VDBE program, and collects column p2 of every OpenRead opcode, i.e. the root page number of each b-tree the statement opens; those get sorted/deduped into State::Monitoring. handle_storage_change then intersects that sorted list against StorageChange::Tables { root_pages_sorted } (via has_sorted_intersection in src/iter.rs), and the producer side of those root pages is Storage::resolve_root_page in src/storage.rs, which walks SQLite ptrmap pages.
questions.why_asked: Reactive queries are SQLSync's headline feature; you need to know whether invalidation is per-table or whole-database before you trust it with a big schema.

questions.text: Do Graft identifiers encode when they were created, how precise is that, and when would it run out?
questions.how_found: Read crates/graft/src/core/gid.rs (16-byte GID = 7-byte time part + 9-byte random part, serialized Base58 as TIME-RANDOM) and then gid/time.rs. GidTimestamp is a 1-byte type prefix plus ts: [u8; 6]: From<SystemTime> takes millis since UNIX_EPOCH as u64 big-endian and keeps only bytes [2..], so 48 bits of milliseconds; as_time reverses it. That is millisecond resolution with room for ~2^48 ms (roughly year 10889), and it is why the string form sorts in ascending chronological order.
questions.why_asked: Volume/Log/Segment ids show up in every log line and every remote object key; knowing the left half is a sortable millisecond clock changes how you debug and how you sort listings.

questions.text: If a database shrinks and then grows back, does the discarded content really disappear?
questions.how_found: Followed the VFS truncate path: graft-sqlite/src/file/vol_file.rs::truncate converts the byte size to a PageCount and calls writer.soft_truncate. The VolumeWrite trait doc in crates/graft/src/volume_writer.rs states it plainly: the operation writes no pages, it only updates the page count, so pages hidden by a smaller count become visible again if the volume is later extended. The impl at lines 75-81 only drops still-uncommitted pages from the in-memory map.
questions.why_asked: Anyone reasoning about VACUUM, about deleting sensitive rows, or about storage cost needs to know that truncation here is a metadata change, not an erase.

questions.text: After the link to the server drops, how long does the browser pause before retrying, and does that pause grow?
questions.how_found: CoordinatorClient in sqlsync-wasm/src/net.rs holds a ConnectionState; the Disconnected arm awaits backoff.wait() before emitting a Connect task, and every error path calls backoff.step(). The bounds are the two constants at the top (10 ms floor, 5000 ms ceiling) and the growth rule is Backoff::step in sqlsync-wasm/src/utils.rs lines 160-165: current_ms *= 2, clamped to max_ms. Note the delay is reset to the floor on a successful Connected -> error transition.
questions.why_asked: When a demo sits there not reconnecting, you need to know whether you're waiting 10 ms or 5 s, and whether the client will hammer the coordinator after an outage.

questions.text: A WebAssembly module can suspend in the middle of a database lookup and continue afterwards; how is that suspension implemented?
questions.how_found: Read lib/sqlsync-reducer/src/guest_reactor.rs. There is no real executor inside the sandbox: raw_query/raw_execute push a Request into a global Reactor keyed by an incrementing RequestId and hand back a ResponseFuture. Reactor::step polls the single boxed task with a noop waker; ResponseFuture::poll returns Pending unless a response with its id has already been delivered, then drains the outgoing Requests map. The host side drives it in a loop: lib/sqlsync/src/reducer.rs WasmReducer::apply calls ffi.reduce, services each Request against the rusqlite Transaction, and calls ffi.reactor_step with the responses until no requests remain.
questions.why_asked: Reducers are the extension point you'll write first, and 'why does my await never finish' is unanswerable until you understand that the host, not the sandbox, is the executor.

questions.text: The Graft extension adds its own pragmas, but SQLite core knows nothing about them. What mechanism actually delivers a custom pragma string to the extension?
questions.how_found: You naturally start in graft: crates/graft-sqlite/src/pragma.rs parses the names and crates/graft-sqlite/src/vfs.rs implements `fn pragma` on the Vfs trait, but nothing in graft calls it. The caller lives in the sqlite-plugin repo: x_file_control intercepts op == SQLITE_FCNTL_PRAGMA, reads the name from args[1] and the optional argument from args[2], calls vfs.pragma(...), and maps PragmaErr::NotFound to SQLITE_NOTFOUND so SQLite falls through to its built-in pragmas; a returned message is copied back into args[0] via sqlite3_mprintf.
questions.why_asked: Adding a new graft_* pragma is a plausible first task, and you cannot do it safely without knowing that the plumbing (and the NotFound fallthrough contract) lives in a different repository.

questions.text: Every Graft commit records exactly which page numbers it touched. Where does that set actually live, and what keeps it from bloating the commit?
questions.how_found: In graft, crates/graft/src/core/commit.rs stores `pageset: PageSet` on SegmentIdx, and crates/graft/src/core/pageset.rs shows PageSet is a thin newtype over splinter_rs::CowSplinter<Bytes>. The compaction itself is in the splinter-rs repo: Partition::optimize_kind estimates the encoded size of each candidate representation (Tree, Vec, Bitmap, Run, plus Empty/Full shortcuts at the top) and switch_kind converts to whichever is smallest; Optimizable::optimize (lines 215-233) optimizes children first so the estimate is accurate. RemoteCommit calls pageset.optimize() right before building the segment (crates/graft/src/rt/action/remote_commit.rs:267).
questions.why_asked: The 'sync only what changed' claim rests entirely on this set staying tiny; before changing commit encoding you need to know the representation is chosen adaptively in another crate, not hardcoded in graft.
